strengths: Addresses a relevant NLP evaluation question: how collaboration settings affect the outputs of interactive qualitative-coding systems. Studying the complete human–system workflow is a worthwhile contribution.

Compares three substantially different approaches—topic modeling, relational inference, and LLM-assisted coding—on a common corpus of approximately 85,000 tweets. Holding initialization fixed within each tool provides some experimental control.

The evaluation usefully distinguishes consistency, cohesiveness, distinctiveness, and assignment correctness. The 1,200-pair human audit, with two annotators and adjudication, and participant interviews provide complementary evidence beyond embedding metrics.

The paper is generally well organized, with accessible descriptions of the systems and evaluation procedures. The appendices document interaction operations, prompt templates, and some implementation settings.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate collaboration modality (Section 4). Asynchronous collaboration is introduced as independent work followed by consolidation, but the experiments compare individual codebooks with three-person synchronous codebooks, without describing consolidation. Team size, aggregation of expertise, and potentially person-hours therefore change alongside synchrony. Participant allocation, reuse across experiments, task order, and time budgets are also unspecified. A comparable asynchronous-team condition, or a substantially narrower interpretation as a team-versus-individual case study, is needed.

The statistical evidence is insufficiently justified. Each tool has only two synchronous and three individual codebooks, yielding one synchronous codebook-pair comparison versus three overlapping asynchronous comparisons. Tables 1–2 report unpaired t-tests without specifying experimental units or sample sizes. Themes and comparisons sharing codebooks cannot simply be treated as independent replications. Analysis respecting this dependence, uncertainty intervals, and treatment of multiple comparisons are needed. This directly weakens the central claim of significant collaboration effects and prevents a sound Findings recommendation as submitted.

The correctness evaluation cannot be reconstructed from the description (Section 5, Figure 4). The plot reports F1, while the protocol describes checking sampled document–theme assignments; reference labels, false negatives, averaging, and sampling weights are undefined. Table 4 reports invalid LLM labels for 0.7–16.1% of documents, but their treatment in evaluation is unclear. Uncertainty intervals are absent. Additionally, the claim that asynchronous topic modeling is more accurate does not match Figure 4: overall scores are equal, and synchronous scores are higher at two intermediate cutoffs.

The proposed framework needs stronger validation as a measure of codebook quality. Maximum theme matching depends on theme number and granularity, yet theme counts, size distributions, and treatment of many-to-one matches are not reported. Centroid similarities remain approximately 0.94–0.98 even when document overlap is low, raising questions about discrimination. Selecting the top 25% using different criteria across systems further complicates comparisons. Sensitivity analyses and human judgments of theme equivalence would help establish what these metrics capture.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite Section 9's assertion. Missing details include the S-BERT checkpoint, LLM decoding settings, selected prompt for each session, prompt-selection sample sizes, resulting codebooks, and sufficient relational-inference configuration. Code and annotation outputs are promised without an accompanying release link. Appendix C also does not report completed-interview counts by condition or the interview-analysis procedure, limiting verification of the comparative user-experience findings.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence. One English vaccine corpus and one implementation per family support a focused case study, while category-wide claims require additional support. Broad conclusions about LLM reliability and expense rest on Llama 3.2 3B-Instruct with verbose prompts, without comparisons establishing whether model choice, prompting, or decoding explains the observed limitations. Similarly, greater interaction bandwidth as the mechanism behind synchronous benefits remains an untested hypothesis. Narrowing these claims would improve alignment between the contribution and its evidence.
